final_text:
The one that matters most is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

Why it stands out for the Marine heatwave early warning project:

- **It's a real-world demonstration of your project's end goal.** The paper documents Australia's first pre-emptive rescue of a protected marine species, triggered *by a marine heatwave forecast* ahead of the 2023/24 El Niño. That's exactly the chain your project is building: forecast → credible early warning → concrete action. It's a working example of what a successful early-warning system looks like in practice.
- **It shows the value of lead time.** The forecast flagged a high-risk MHW before it hit, an expert workshop assessed the threat, and 25 red handfish were removed from the wild in January 2024 — just in time, as in-situ temperatures then exceeded records (80 days more than 2°C above the long-term mean summer temperature). The paper makes the case that the intervention "bought time," which is the argument for investing in better, earlier forecasts.
- **It's a conservation hook for your lab's stakeholders.** If you're pitching the project to coastal managers or funders, this is a concrete, recent, published case where a forecast directly saved a Critically Endangered species — strong evidence that early warning has tangible value.

The runner-up is **#5** (Mojumder, 2026), which is directly on-topic — it evaluates 1–14-day machine-learning MHW forecasts against persistence benchmarks in the Northern Bay of Bengal, so it's useful for the forecasting-methods side of your project. But it's a B.S. thesis data release (Zenodo), so it's more of a methods reference than a strategic one. #4 is the paper that tells you *why* the project matters; #5 tells you *how* to test your forecasts.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

The clearest fit is **#4** — "Code and aggregated results for 'A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea'" (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it matters most for Plastic pathways:

- **It is the only item on the slate that is directly about marine litter.** The rest touch the project at best indirectly — #12 (loggerhead turtle habitat use) and #11 (lake hydroclimatic trends) are about other species or systems, and #3, #9 are about phytoplankton production.
- **It is a methods resource, not just a paper.** It ships the actual three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, the experiment scripts, and the aggregated result files behind every number in the manuscript (#4, abstract). If the team is running or planning particle-tracking experiments for debris pathways, this is directly reusable code.
- **It is validated against field records.** The kernel was developed and tested against beaching records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories (#4, setting) — a concrete example of the kind of field-validated pathway modeling the project is about.
- **It is current and open.** Deposited 2026 and still open (#4), so it is fresh and the underlying data (trajectories, flow fields) are available on request.

One caveat: I could not see the project's confirmed state (goals, blockers, milestones) in this conversation, so I am judging fit from the project's name and the lab's declared interest in debris pathways. If the team has a specific open blocker — say, a beaching or deposition model to validate — #4 is the item that speaks to it.

Suggested next steps (edits happen in the app, not here):
- Have Jonah or Priya skim #4's README and kernel code to see if the OceanParcels setup maps onto what the project is running.
- If it does, request the trajectory and ROMS flow-field data to benchmark against.

Here's the comparison:

**#1 – A stronger Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)**
This is a large infrastructure and governance call. It's about deploying observation equipment, running observing system experiments, network optimization, and co-creating technology roadmaps with industry — all to strengthen the GOOS framework and reduce dependency on non-EU partners. The emphasis is on *building and sustaining the observation backbone itself*: sensors, networks, data delivery, and the governance structures around them.

**#2 – Unlocking a safe operating space for Antarctica and the Southern Ocean (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)**
This is a research call focused on *understanding and projecting* the future of the Southern Ocean: ocean–atmosphere–sea ice–ice dynamics, tipping points, extreme events, ecosystem vulnerability, and improving Earth System Models and regional coupled models. It explicitly calls for work on extreme events and mid-latitude weather, and for reducing uncertainties in projected future changes.

**Which fits Marine heatwave early warning better?**

**#2 is the stronger fit.** Your project is about *forecasting* marine heatwaves — predicting them, evaluating ML forecast methods, and triggering rapid response. That's squarely in #2's territory: improving projections, understanding extreme events, reducing uncertainties in future changes, and advancing models (including regional coupled models). The call's explicit mention of "extreme events and mid-latitude weather" and "improving Earth System Models and regional coupled models" maps directly onto what your team is doing with ML-based heatwave forecasts.

#1 is more about the *observation infrastructure* that feeds forecasts — sensors, networks, data pipelines. While your project certainly depends on good observations, the grant is asking for proposals to *build and sustain* that infrastructure, not to develop forecasting methods or understand climate dynamics. It's a good fit if you were leading a sensor-deployment or data-delivery work package, but it's not where the forecasting science lives.

One practical note: #1 has a much earlier deadline (Feb 2027) and a much larger budget (€50M vs €5–11M), which suggests it's likely a flagship or FET-style call requiring a larger consortium. #2's smaller size and later deadline (Sep 2027) may be more realistic for a three-person lab to lead, though you'd still need partners for the multidisciplinary scope.

Now I have everything I need. Let me synthesize the answer.

Here's what I found, Mara.

## Best-fitting open grant: #21 — Microplastics Research and Resource Coordination Center

Of everything I checked, **#21** is the closest match to the Plastic pathways project. It's a US NIEHS U24 coordination center for micro/nanoplastics research, focused on standardizing sampling and analytical methods, harmonizing data, and fostering multidisciplinary collaboration across the M/NPs field. The project's core work — marine litter tracking, Lagrangian particle tracking, floating debris detection, satellite remote sensing, and beaching — sits squarely in the space this call is trying to organize.

**Deadline:** 2026-12-01 — that's about three weeks away, so it's the most time-pressured of the open options.

**The biggest doubt:** the call is framed around *health effects* of M/NPs and biomedical/material-science standardization, while the project is more about *pathways, transport, and detection*. The fit is real but not airtight — the proposal would need to angle the work toward standardizing how the field samples, detects, and tracks plastics in the environment, which is doable but requires a deliberate framing choice.

### Other open grants on the project's slate, briefly:

- **#27** (Global Ocean Observing System, €50M, deadline 2027-02-16) — broad ocean observation infrastructure; the project's satellite and data-assimilation work fits, but it's a much bigger, more systems-level call.
- **#29** (Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity, €3–8M, deadline 2027-09-22) — strong methodological overlap with the project's satellite remote sensing and data-integration work, but the focus is biodiversity, not plastic pathways.
- **#2** (Novel recycling technologies for complex plastics, €3–8M, deadline 2027-09-22) — about biotech recycling of plastic *materials*, a different angle from tracking and pathways.
- **#19** (Waterborne transport environmental impact, €2–13.5M, deadline 2027-04-14) — about zero-carbon fuel pollution in shipping, adjacent but not the same problem.

## Who in the lab should lead

The people-for-call analysis for #21 shows **no one's declared profile covers any of its slots** (health effects of M/NPs, sampling/analytical standardization, data harmonization, distribution of experimental standards). That's a gap, not a disqualifier — it means the lead would be setting new ground.

That said, the strongest internal candidates, based on what I can see:

- **Jonah Whitcombe (#15)** — declared interests in *marine litter* and *Lagrangian analysis*. He is the only lab member whose declared profile directly names the subject matter of the project. He'd be the natural scientific lead on the plastic-pathways content.
- **Priya Raman (#16)** — declared interests in *satellite oceanography* and *coastal water quality*. The project's satellite remote sensing and detection work is her declared territory, and the call's emphasis on standardizing sampling and analytical methods would benefit from her observational expertise.
- **You (#14)** — as PI and project owner, you'd likely be the overall lead or co-lead, especially given the data-assimilation and ML angle that the project's method concepts include.

The nightly ranking for #29 (the biodiversity remote-sensing call) named Priya and Sun-hee as closest profile matches, which suggests the lab's remote-sensing and data-tools strengths are recognized. For #21 specifically, the ranking didn't name anyone, consistent with the slot gaps.

**My read:** Jonah should lead the scientific content (he's the marine-litter person), you should lead the overall proposal as PI, and Priya should anchor the remote-sensing and detection methodology. Sun-hee's data-tools background would be valuable for the data-harmonization component the call asks for.

## Who outside the lab could partner

This is where I have to be honest: **collaborator search is turned off on this instance**, so I can't see co-authorship chains or external people who've consented to be suggested. The introduction-path lookups for Jonah and Priya returned no visible chains.

What I can say from what's visible: the call explicitly asks for a *coordination center* that brings together biomedical and material-science researchers. The lab's profile is ocean-science-heavy, so the natural external partners would be groups working on the *health-effects* and *analytical-chemistry* side of M/NPs — the slots no one in the lab covers. If you have existing collaborators in environmental toxicology, analytical chemistry, or public health who've worked on plastics, they'd fill those gaps. But I can't name specific people or labs from what I can see here.

If you'd like, you could turn on collaborator search in the app settings, and I could then look for concrete external partners with the right expertise.

results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

It is essential to better understand the roles of anthropogenic and natural drivers of carbon fluxes, in particular the surface-to-air flux. The European Union aims to protect and conserve its marine and freshwater environments by achieving Good Environmental and Good Ecological Status[1]. The European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact further emphasize the need to enhance the resilience of European waters to human-induced pressures. Projects like the Horizon Europe EMERGE have researched the impacts of shipping on marine ecosystems. The introduction of technologies to decarbonize the sector may enable, to a certain extent, to phase-out relevant current sources of water and air pollution. However, renewable low and zero-carbon fuels and procedures pose new risks to marine and other aquatic ecosystems like rivers and lakes yet to be explored and addressed, both from the normal function of waterborne transport[2] and from accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels. In addition, other pollution sources can be addressed today[3]. This topic aims to evaluate, forecast, control and mitigate the impact of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, with a focus on developing and demonstrating innovative abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to mitigate and eliminate, where possible, the harmful impact of waterborne transport in the ocean and inland waters. New technologies and solutions addressing the decarbonization of waterborne transport will be considered, as well as the potential risks and challenges associated with these.

Actions should address all of the following aspects:

- Evaluate and forecast the environmental impacts of waterborne transport operations on marine, rivers and other aquatic ecosystems, in particular regarding the effects of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels (with particular attention to accidental spills) and related technologies. The proposal may include testing and experimental work in relation with spills.

- Develop and demonstrate effective response scenarios, including the associated abatement technologies and any potential new innovative equipment, for managing uncontrolled releases of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels in marine and inland waters or in port areas, including dedicated specific procedures and operational guidelines.

- Modelling scenarios on water and air pollution sources from each ship types and services running on renewable low and zero carbon fuels.

- Develop and demonstrate innovative and cost-effective abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to prevent, eliminate and reduce the harmful impacts of the use of renewable low and zero carbon fuels. Relevant TRL5 demonstration of such systems should be done.

- Identifying training needs and skills requirements to deploy developed solutions, as well as in relation to the management and use of renewable low carbon fuels in ports and on vessels in marine and inland waters, including relevant emergency response preparedness.

final_text:
Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, plus the papers and a funding angle.

## Where the project stands
It's a lab project with three members — Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you. Mycelium holds its working scope as:
- **Beaching** and **marine litter tracking**
- **Lagrangian particle tracking**
- **Floating debris detection**
- **Satellite ocean remote sensing**

One thing worth flagging: two of those concepts — *floating debris detection* and *Lagrangian particle tracking* — aren't declared in any member's profile. That's a gap to either fill (someone should own it) or a profile to update, so the project's slate keeps matching well.

## Three most relevant new papers
1. **#7 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026). The closest match: a three-phase beaching kernel plus particle kernels for OceanParcels, validated against field records from Uido, Korea. Directly on your beaching + particle-tracking core.
2. **#12 — "Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026). A YOLO11-based detection/segmentation framework for low-contrast, curved features in satellite imagery — a useful methodological template for your floating-debris-detection work.
3. **#6 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model"** (Zhang, 2026). A Zenodo data/code deposit for a regional ocean forecast system. Relevant as the flow-field / model-data side of particle tracking, though it's the thinnest of the three (no abstract in the record, so I can't say more than that).

The other new slate items (#5 Arctic LiDAR phytoplankton, #9 NE Pacific seasonal forecast, #11 multi-agent tracking) are off-topic for this project.

## One funding opportunity
**#10 — NSF Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC)** — deadline **2027-02-15**. It funds unsolicited proposals for instrumentation and technology development with broad applicability to ocean science. A natural fit: the *tide-resolving beaching kernel* (#7) is exactly the kind of reusable, broadly applicable tool OTIC looks for, and you could frame a proposal around developing/validating a next-generation beaching-and-tracking kernel for marine litter.

A larger, more ambitious alternative is **#3 — the EU's €50M Global Ocean Observing System call** (deadline 2027-02-16), but that's a consortium-scale observing-infrastructure bid rather than a single-lab project, so OTIC is the more realistic first target.

Want me to pull the full text of #7 to see exactly how the beaching kernel is built, or dig into the OTIC program's evaluation criteria?

#12 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Authors: Zhenhua Zhang, Peng Chen, Siqi Zhang, Delu Pan
Venue: Science Advances
Year: 2026

Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The authors used 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP). A bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions, and low-light estimates were generated as physically const…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Arctic region, specifically marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions, using spaceborne LiDAR data from 2006 to 2023.
Abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year −1 during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

#36 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#39 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

The paper that matters most for the Marine heatwave early warning project is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

**Why it stands out:**

1. **It's a real-world proof of concept for your project's core idea.** The paper documents Australia's first pre-emptive rescue of a protected marine species, triggered *by a marine heatwave forecast* ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño. An expert workshop assessed the forecasted extremes (>20°C or +~3°C) as a severe threat, and that assessment triggered the emergency action. This is exactly the "early warning → rapid response" loop your project is building toward.

2. **It shows the full chain working end-to-end:** forecast → expert risk assessment → approval → intervention → post-release survival confirmation. The 18 fish released after the MHW subsided had survival confirmed two months later. That's a complete, documented cycle of forecast-driven action, not just a model evaluation.

3. **It's directly relevant to your lab's mission.** Your project is about early warning for marine heatwaves; this paper demonstrates what happens when that warning is actually *used* — it changes decisions, saves individuals, and provides a template for proactive conservation during climate extremes.

**The other strong candidate** is **#5** (Mojumder, 2026), which evaluates 1–14-day ML forecasts of MHWs against persistence benchmarks in the Northern Bay of Bengal. That's methodologically useful for your forecasting pipeline, but it's a thesis code/data release with a thin abstract — less actionable than #4's concrete demonstration of forecast-to-action.

If you want, I can pull the full text of #4 to dig into the forecast details (what system produced the El Niño warning, lead times, thresholds) or the decision-making protocol they used.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

One caveat: the project's confirmed state (goals, method, blockers) is not visible to me in this conversation, so I am judging fit from the project's name and the slate itself. Here's the comparison.

**#1 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)**
This is about the *infrastructure* of ocean observation: deploying equipment, running observing system experiments, network optimization, and co-creating technology roadmaps with industry. The focus is on filling structural gaps in under-observed regions (deep sea, polar) and strengthening the GOOS framework under IOC-UNESCO. It's a big, systems-level call — €50M — aimed at stabilizing and operationalizing the global observing backbone, with a strong governance and strategic-autonomy angle.

**#2 — Unlocking a safe operating space for Antarctica and the Southern Ocean (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)**
This is a *science* call: resolving uncertainties and improving projections of the Antarctic/Southern Ocean, with explicit attention to extreme events, ocean circulation, tipping elements, and ecosystem vulnerability. It calls for improving Earth System Models and regional coupled models, developing monitoring indicators, and distinguishing human-induced from natural change.

**Which fits Marine heatwave early warning (#3) better?**

**#2 is the better fit.** Here's why:

- **Method alignment:** Your project is about *forecasting* marine heatwaves — short-to-medium-range prediction, ML-based forecasting, and triggering rapid response. #2 explicitly asks for improved projections, better understanding of extreme events, and enhanced Earth System Models and regional coupled models. That's the same methodological territory.
- **Scope alignment:** #2's scope includes "extreme events and mid-latitude weather" and "abrupt, irreversible change/tipping elements and thresholds" — marine heatwaves sit squarely in that space.
- **Scale and timeline:** At €5–11M with a September 2027 deadline, #2 is a more natural size for a 3-person lab project focused on a specific forecasting problem. #1 at €50M is a consortium-scale infrastructure call that would require a much broader team and a heavier governance/observation-network component.

**Where #1 could still play a role:** If your project has a strong data-assimilation or observing-system-experiment component (e.g., you're building or evaluating the observation networks that feed your forecasts), #1's emphasis on OSSEs, network optimization, and data delivery could be relevant. But the core of #1 is about *building and sustaining the observing infrastructure itself*, not about the forecasting science that uses those observations.

**Bottom line:** Lead with #2. It matches your project's method (forecasting, extreme events, model improvement), its scale, and its timeline. #1 is a possible secondary target if you want to frame a component around observing-system design, but it's a bigger, more infrastructure-heavy call.

Now I have a clear picture. Let me put together the recommendation.

---

## Best-fitting open grant: #21 — *Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate*

**Why it fits best:**

- **Problem match:** The call explicitly asks for improved prediction, projection, and attribution of extreme events, with a specific emphasis on *early warning systems* — which is exactly what the Marine heatwave early warning project (#7) is building. Marine heatwaves are a canonical extreme event, and the call welcomes AI-based approaches, which is the project's core method.
- **Method match:** The call asks for a hierarchy of models (including high-resolution Earth system models and digital twins), AI-based approaches, quantitative intercomparisons, and retrospective analyses. The project's slate already includes ML forecast evaluation (#12), multi-horizon operational forecasting (#24), and subseasonal skill assessment (#25) — all directly relevant.
- **Scale and deadline:** €3M–€15M, deadline **2027-03-04** — enough runway to build a consortium.
- **Integration hooks:** The call encourages cooperation with Copernicus, Destination Earth, and low- to middle-income countries, and selected proposals may involve the JRC. This opens doors to operational partners and international collaborators.

**Why not the others:**
- **#15 (GOOS, €50M, deadline 2027-02-16):** Broadly about strengthening the *observing system* — instrumentation, OSEs/OSSEs, network optimisation, areas beyond national jurisdiction. The project's focus is *forecasting and early warning*, not building observing infrastructure. The fit is indirect.
- **#10 (NSF OTIC, deadline 2027-02-15):** About *instrumentation development* with broad applicability. No one in the lab has a declared instrumentation-development profile, and the project is about forecasting, not building instruments.
- **#20 (Biodiversity data integration, deadline 2027-09-22):** About integrating omics/in-situ biodiversity data with remote sensing. Adjacent but not the project's core.

---

## Who in the lab should lead

**You (Mara Ellison)** should lead the application. Here's why:

- The nightly ranking names you first for #21: your integration of data assimilation with ML for ocean forecasting directly addresses the call's demand for "seamless prediction and projection modelling capabilities."
- You are the PI and project owner of #7, so you own the scientific narrative.
- Your declared interests (data assimilation with ML, ocean extremes) map onto the call's two main axes: AI-based prediction methods and extreme events.

**Co-leads / key contributors:**

| Person | Role in the application | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Tomás Ferreira-Lind** (#6) | Co-lead on the modelling/physics side. His declared interest in *regional ocean models* covers the call's "Earth system models" slot, and his physics-informed ML surrogates are directly relevant to the "AI-based approaches" the call welcomes. | Declared: regional ocean models; physics-informed ML |
| **Sun-hee Park** (#5) | Lead on the operational/data-tools side. Her declared interest in *ocean data tools* supports the call's emphasis on operational early warning systems and integration with Copernicus. | Declared: ocean data tools |
| **Priya Raman** (#4) | Contributes the satellite/remote-sensing perspective, which the call values for multi-sensor data integration and for the ESA FutureEO coordination it mentions. | Declared: satellite oceanography, coastal water quality |
| **Jonah Whitcombe** (#3) | Contributes the Lagrangian/marine-litter angle if the application wants to discuss cascading impacts of heatwaves on coastal ecosystems and debris transport. | Declared: marine litter, Lagrangian analysis |

**Gaps to fill externally:** The call asks for *digital twins*, *Copernicus integration*, and *Destination Earth* experience — no one in the lab declares these. You'll want at least one partner with operational Copernicus or Destination Earth experience.

---

## Who outside the lab to partner with

Based on the papers on the project's slate and the call's requirements, here are the most natural external partners:

1. **NOAA / GFDL (Northeast Pacific seasonal ocean forecasting team)** — Authors of #9 (seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific, MOM6 + SIS2 + COBALT, forced by GFDL-SPEAR). They have operational seasonal ocean forecasts going live in October 2026, which is exactly the kind of "seamless prediction" infrastructure the call asks for. They could anchor the *operational forecasting* work package and bring the Copernicus/US integration angle.

2. **South Korean aquaculture forecasting group (Kang, Kim, Jeong — #24)** — They built the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture, with a demonstrated 38-hour advisory lead time. They are a natural partner for the *AI-based early warning* work package and bring a low- to middle-income-country-adjacent operational use case (the call explicitly encourages international cooperation for capacity building).

3. **Adriatic Sea MHW group (Liyana, Memmola, Falco — #26)** — They combine high-resolution ROMS with eddy diagnostics for MHW detection in a semi-enclosed basin. They could anchor a *regional case study* work package and bring the Mediterranean/Copernicus Marine Service connection.

4. **Tropical Indian Ocean subseasonal MHW group (Meng, Li, Yan — #25)** — They evaluate subseasonal MHW forecast skill in the tropical Indian Ocean. A natural partner for the *subseasonal-to-seasonal prediction* work package and for the international cooperation angle (India is eligible for Horizon Europe funding).

5. **GOOS / IOC community (authors of #32, the GOOS Status Report 2026)** — Belbéoch, Begg, Fournier, Kolodziejczyk, Post, Prakash, Rusciano, Stukonytė. They are the natural partners for the *observing system and data infrastructure* work package, and can help address the call's emphasis on GOOS coordination and data sharing.

6. **JRC (European Commission Joint Research Centre)** — The call explicitly says selected proposals may involve the JRC for scientific advice and technical support in the context of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service. This is a low-cost, high-credibility addition that also covers the "Copernicus" gap no one in the lab declares.

---

**Suggested consortium shape:**

| Work package | Lead | Key partners |
|---|---|---|
| AI-based MHW prediction & early warning | You (Mara) | Kang et al. (#24), Tomás |
| Operational forecasting & Copernicus integration | Sun-hee | NOAA/GFDL (#9), JRC |
| Regional case studies (Adriatic, Indian Ocean) | Priya | Liyana et al. (#26), Meng et al. (#25) |
| Observing system & data infrastructure | Tomás | GOOS/IOC community (#32) |

#11 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#24 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for a comprehensive overview of the status, coverage, and sustainability of the global ocean observing system, including gaps in capacity and funding.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Compilation of an interactive status report aggregating statistics on national contributions, monitoring data from 17 GOOS observing networks via OceanOPS, satellite observations, and data from marine life initiatives, supplemented by qualitative impact stories.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean observations from the seafloor to the atmosphere, involving 67 countries, 17 GOOS observing networks, satellite systems, and diverse marine ecosystem initiatives.
Abstract:
The ocean underpins the safety, wellbeing and livelihoods of communities worldwide. Understanding how it is changing depends on sustained ocean observations: the measurements collected by dedicated people, instruments and platforms, from the seafloor to the atmosphere. The Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) Status Report 2026 provides an interactive overview of the status of the global ocean observing system, presents new statistics on national contributions, and showcases the societal value of ocean observations through impact stories from around the globe. Today, 67 countries contribute to physical and biogeochemical ocean observations at sea through 17 GOOS observing networks monitored by OceanOPS. Satellites complement these measurements with observations from space, while a diverse community of initiatives collects vital data on marine life and ecosystems. Together, these observations underpin weather forecasting, climate monitoring, maritime and coastal risk management, biodiversity conservation and sustainable ocean economies. The global ocean observing system continues to make progress, supported by established observing networks, long-term reference observatories, regional systems and emerging technologies. Yet, important gaps and risks remain. Observing capacity is unevenly distributed around the world, and many networks face challenges in securing the sustained funding needed to maintain and expand their observations. Strengthening coordination, improving data sharing and broadening international participation will be essential to build a more comprehensive, resilient and sustainable system. Continued investment and stronger collaboration across countries and observing communities are crucial to ensure that ocean observations can meet growing scientific, operational and societal needs. Explore the interactive GOOS Status Report to find out more.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

#26 [paper] Model-Based Marine Heatwave Detection with Eddy Diagnostics in the Adriatic Sea: Regional Insights with Global Relevance
Authors: Eurida Liyana, Francesco Memmola, Pierpaolo Falco
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15010054/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The intensification, increasing frequency, and duration of marine heatwave (MHW) events, particularly in vulnerable semi-enclosed coastal basins like the Adriatic Sea.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Integration of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm and analysis of long-term observational temperature data.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Adriatic Sea (AS).
Abstract:
Marine heatwave (MHW) events are intensifying globally, doubling in frequency and increasing in duration and spatial distribution over recent decades. Semi-enclosed coastal basins are particularly vulnerable, and the Adriatic Sea (AS) exemplifies a fast-reacting system, making it a natural laboratory for studying climate-driven ocean variability and impacts on ecosystems, fisheries, and aquaculture. In this study, we assess the capability of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) to detect and simulate MHW events in the AS. We integrate this modeling framework with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm, alongside comprehensive analysis of long-term observational temperature data, to investigate the role of mesoscale eddies in modulating surface and subsurface MHW evolution. Results demonstrate that ROMS effectively reproduces the timing and spatial patterns of historical MHWs in the AS, showing strong agreement between modeled and observed MHWs, with eddy structures frequently coinciding with subsurface thermal anomalies preceding MHWs. These findings highlight the value of coupling regional ocean models with mesoscale eddy diagnostics to advance understanding of MHW occurrences and drivers, and to strengthen early-warning capabilities. Enhanced understanding of MHW precursors and eddy interactions in the AS provides a pathway for anticipating hazards, informing adaptive measures for coastal stakeholders, and improving regional climate resilience. Beyond the Adriatic, this framework offers a transferable approach to other semi-enclosed and shelf seas, where reliable detection of MHW drivers is essential. By linking detection with predictive understanding, this work contributes to broader efforts to improve preparedness for marine extremes and safeguard ecosystems and dependent economies in a warming ocean.

---

## Best-fitting open grant: #9 — Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)

**Why it fits Plastic pathways better than #16:**

- **#9** is about strengthening the global ocean observing system — deploying observation equipment, running observing system experiments, network optimisation, and co-creating technology roadmaps. The Plastic pathways project (marine litter dispersal, beaching, Lagrangian tracking) sits naturally inside this: you need better observations of where debris goes, and the grant explicitly calls for filling structural gaps in under-observed regions. The lab's declared strengths in satellite oceanography and data assimilation map directly onto the "strengthen and operationalise the observing system" slot.
- **#16** (NSF OTIC) is specifically about *instrumentation development* with broad applicability. No one in the lab has a declared profile in instrumentation development, and the nightly ranking only found weak profile matches (62–65%). It's a harder fit.

**Gaps in #9 that no one in the lab covers:**
- Observing system experiments (OSEs) / simulation experiments (OSSEs)
- Network optimisation approaches
- Areas beyond national jurisdiction
- Industry co-creation (the grant explicitly asks for industry partners)

---

## Who should lead the application

**Priya Raman (#4)** is the strongest lead:
- Declared interests: Satellite oceanography, Coastal water quality
- The nightly ranking named her first for #9: her satellite ocean colour remote sensing work contributes directly to the "strengthened global ocean observing capacities and data coordination" slot.
- She's already a member of the Plastic pathways project.

**You (Mara Ellison, #2)** are the natural co-lead / PI:
- The ranking named you second: your data assimilation + ML for ocean forecasting "enhances the resilience and accuracy of the observing system's outputs."
- As PI and project owner, you'd anchor the proposal's scientific direction.

**Jonah Whitcombe (#3)** should be a core co-PI:
- Declared interests: Marine litter, Lagrangian analysis — the most direct match to the project's subject matter.
- He's already on the project.

**Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#6)** could strengthen the physics/ML angle (circulation and turbulence, physics-informed ML), which supports the model-based components of the proposal.

**Sun-hee Park (#5)** (ocean data tools) could contribute to the data infrastructure / delivery side the grant asks for.

---

## Potential external partners

From the papers on the project's slate, three groups stand out:

1. **Sehan Lim & Sunwook Hong** (#13) — developed a tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter using OceanParcels and ROMS flow fields, applied to field records in Korea. Their work is methodologically close to what Plastic pathways does (Lagrangian particle tracking of debris) and they have open code. A partnership would add a validated beaching kernel and a non-EU field site.

2. **Hilaire Amemou, Philippe Cecchi, Vamara Koné, Pierrick Penven, Christophe Lett** (#20) — modelled plastic dispersal and beaching along the Côte d'Ivoire coast using Ichthyop + CROCO. This is a direct methodological peer group (Lagrangian particle tracking for plastic) and a West African site that would help address the grant's call for "structural gaps in under-observed regions."

3. **Valeria Teso, Diego Urteaga, et al.** (#23) — ROV survey of deep-sea marine litter in the Mar del Plata Submarine Canyon (Argentina). This adds a deep-sea / canyon dimension and a South American site, which would help cover the "areas beyond national jurisdiction" gap that no one in the lab currently covers.

**Caveat:** None of these external authors are in Mycelium's network, so I can't see introduction paths or whether they're already collaborating with anyone you know. You'd need to reach out directly — the papers are all 2026 and the authors are active.

---

**Suggested next step:** If you want, I can pull the full text of any of these papers to dig into methods, or I can look at the #9 grant's full scope text to map out a section-by-section fit for the proposal.

Abstract:
Plastic pollution is a growing concern in West Africa's marine environment, yet the processes governing its fate remain poorly understood. The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire is particularly vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs from rivers and lagoons. This study investigates the dispersal and coastal retention of urban plastic debris using a Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO). We provide the first regional-scale assessment of seasonal beaching dynamics along the Ivorian coast using a high-resolution coupled hydrodynamic-Lagrangian framework. Simulations show that while a large fraction of particles is transported offshore (~52%), a substantial proportion (~48%) remains nearshore and beaches at least once. Persistent accumulation hotspots are identified around Abidjan, regardless of the release location. Seasonal variability strongly controls debris pathways. During the minor upwelling season (January-April), beaching occurs predominantly west of Abidjan, associated with weaker currents and enhanced coastal retention. In contrast, during the major upwelling season (June-September), intensified currents and mesoscale activity promote wider dispersal and shift beaching eastward. From October to December, beaching intensifies along the eastern coastline. These results highlight the dominant role of regional hydrodynamics in shaping marine debris distribution and demonstrate the value of high-resolution Lagrangian modeling for identifying pollution hotspots and supporting mitigation strategies in data-scarce coastal regions.

#23 [paper] Out of sight, hidden into the deep: Marine litter in the Mar del Plata Submarine Canyon (southwestern Atlantic) revealed by ROV survey
Authors: Valeria Teso, Diego Urteaga, Graziella Bozzano, Gregório Bigatti, Martín Brogger, Francisco Brusa, Rodrigo Calderón, NADIA CERINO
Venue: PLoS ONE
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0357098
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The deep sea is increasingly recognized as vulnerable to anthropogenic pressures, including marine litter, yet large geographic gaps remain in our understanding of litter distribution and ecological interactions. Submarine canyon systems can act as conduits and accumulation zones for anthropogenic material, but data from the southwestern Atlantic are scarce. Here, we present the first characterization of deep-sea marine macro-litter in the Mar del Plata Submarine Canyon (Argentina), based on 240 hours of remotely operated vehicle (ROV) video collected during 17 dives (878-3,820 m depth) aboard the R/V Falkor (too) in July-August 2025. Litter was observed during 10 dives, comprising 29 items distributed between 1,120 and 3,820 m. Plastic was the dominant material (27 items), followed by rubber (2 items). Most litter consisted of plastic sheets and bags, food wrappers, and commercial fishing-related gear, including lines, ropes, and cables. Litter was observed in multiple settings, including buried or degraded items, resting on the seabed, and trapped among rocks or drifting near the bottom. Most items were located within the canyon domain, forming localized clusters along the canyon axis and walls. Litter-fauna interactions were documented for seven items and included both sessile colonization and associations with mobile fauna, mainly on partially buried plastic items and entangled fishing-related gear. These patterns suggest that substrate stability and residence time may influence sessile colonization. The composition and distribution of debris indicate that maritime activities, particularly fisheries, are the most likely sources and further support the role of submarine canyons as accumulation zones for marine litter. This study provides critical baseline data in an understudied region and highlights the need for improved monitoring programs and management strategies for marine litter to reduce impacts in submarine canyon systems.

Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, what's new for it, and one funding option — corrected.

## Where the project stands

I have to be straight with you: Mylo holds very little confirmed state for this project. What I can see is:

- **Members:** Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you (#2)
- **No confirmed problem, method, stage, milestones, or blockers** are recorded, and I can't see when the state was last confirmed — so anything you've discussed in meetings or docs isn't in Mylo yet.

The project sits under the lab's "Debris pathways" cluster (marine litter tracking, #13), which matches the lab's stated aim of forecasting "where floating debris ends up." If you'd like Mylo to reflect the project's actual state, that's something you can edit in the app — I can't change it for you.

## Three most relevant new papers

All three entered the project's slate this week:

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The most directly on-target: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields. It's a ready-made method and codebase for modelling how litter moves and where it strands — exactly the "pathways" question.

2. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, *Remote Sensing*). Relevant on the observation side: a YOLO11-based framework (YOLO11-ISW) for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, which the authors report achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the methods they evaluated. The pattern — ML for automated, large-scale satellite monitoring — is transferable to detecting and tracking floating debris from space.

3. **#5 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model"** (2026). Relevant as the forcing layer: daily ocean model analyses are the kind of flow fields you'd drive particle-tracking experiments with, as #6 does with ROMS.

(Also on the slate: #4, #7, #9, #11 — but those are phytoplankton, a comment, and computer-vision work with weaker ties to debris pathways.)

## One funding opportunity

**#8 — Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC), NSF** — still open, deadline **15 February 2027**.

- **Why it fits:** OTIC supports unsolicited proposals for instrumentation and technology development with broad applicability to ocean science. A plastic-pathways project that builds or refines particle-tracking kernels, satellite-detection pipelines, or a debris-forecasting tool for coastal managers (#13) is squarely in that lane — it's a technology with community-wide use, not a single study.
- **Biggest doubt:** OTIC leans toward *instrumentation and tool development*. If the project's current emphasis is more on a specific regional study than on a reusable tool, the proposal would need to be framed around the technology contribution. I also can't see the full eligibility rules (institution type, citizenship requirements) from here, so check the program description (PD-98-1680) before committing.

A longer-horizon alternative worth noting: **#12 — "Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity"** (€3–8M, deadline 22 September 2027) — a strong fit if the project can be framed around marine ecosystems under pressure and FAIR data integration, but it's a bigger, more competitive call.

**Suggested next steps:** confirm the project's state in the app so Mylo can track it properly; read #6's code deposit to see if the beaching kernel fits your setup; and if OTIC appeals, start scoping the technology story now — February 2027 is closer than it looks.

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.
